questions.evidenceQuote: Kepler was the leading mathematician of his time, so he probably had a very good sense of probability theorems. In statistics, there is a famous problem called the “secretary problem.” In this task, you are supposed to make the best possible hiring decision based on a series of interviews. Researchers measure how many candidates from a set pool you interview before deciding to hire a particular individual.

questions.evidenceQuote: You cannot go back to previous interviewees, and you must make binary decisions (yes or no) until you make a yes (hire) decision. Computer simulations show that the optimal strategy here is to interview the first 37 percent of candidates (i.e., saying no to all of them) and from that point on decide whether a new candidate is better than the best of the first 37 percent. This is called the “37 percent rule.” How many people actually follow the 37 percent rule?

specificFindings: Researchers measure candidates interviewed before the hiring decision from a set pool. Pool is the candidate set,not a literal place,and the quantity is neither only quality rank nor post-hire interviews.
The model prohibits returning to past interviewees and requires binary yes/no decisions until a hire. These are described task constraints,not website actions to be carried out on actual people.
The37percent strategy rejects an initial comparison sample then judges later candidates against its best. It is not a hire quota,fixed37th candidate or automatic hire from the rejected initial group.

How many actually follow asks empirical adoption after model optimality. The current parent ends with this question,so the exercise tests that transition rather than fabricating a count absent from the excerpt.

The100-potential-mates and37-sampling example is hypothetical,not user relationship history or an actual100-person survey. Probably not is qualified author expectation,not nobody ever or a measured50percent result.

Wasted means effort failing to obtain its intended benefit in the considered situation,not necessarily physical injury or cash alone. The previous rejection antecedent is not fully restated in the short parent,so its question tests lexical meaning rather than inventing missing history.
SP card-flipping experiments minimize extra search costs compared with arranging dates. Minimize/little do not establish mathematically zero costs or identical real-world choice conditions.

Experimental rule-following rates are30percent college students and17percent pigeons. The strategy name37percent is not the student adherence rate. Failure to consistently use a solution is not never selecting or never succeeding.

Herbranson and colleagues report a common pattern of premature selections before the ideal sample size. This is distinguished from economists attributed interpretation of real mate search and Cohen/Todds later CDC-data analysis.

For most people limits the authors directional exploration generalisation. It does not guarantee perfect decisions,erase search/rejection costs or establish indefinite searching as best for every individual.
Cohen and Todd analyse nationally representative CDC-collected observational data. The source roles are not reversed into personally generated random marriage-duration assignments.

The reported contrast includes both search duration and number of dating partners. Longer/several versus shorter/few describes some and others,not a fixed twelve for all or a forced individual life classification.
Animal behaviour literature and computer simulations suggest more errors under insufficient search. These are distinct evidence sources,not CDC data predicting an individuals future relationship.

One mate far better is a hypothetical exception making choice obvious. The real-context many-small-differences premise supports the authors argument for more comparison,not a universal ranking task assigned to the user.

On average marital stability is a group-level association in the reported observational data. No randomised duration intervention,guaranteed divorce prevention or exact37percent necessity is inferred.

Consistent with the rule indicates compatibility,not proof of its precise threshold for all real relationships. However and take issue introduce Todd/Miller qualifications; grounds means reasons,not physical terrain.
One of the best/top10percent changes the success criterion from unique best. The elliptical is picks up critical from the prior discussion; no new unstated numerical quality measure is added.

With1000 options,the target is top10percent and initial search3percent; with100 options,the text discusses14percent. Pool size,quality percentile and sample proportion are not exchanged. Highest model probability is not certainty.

A lot more reasonable is a practical assessment of reduced initial search,not proof every relationship is guaranteed or a measured brain difference. The stable source is a phrase fragment in the printed text.
Take a dozen is attributed to Todd and Miller as doing a pretty good job of finding a top10percent option,not a universal unique-best theorem or simultaneous hiring of twelve people.

The application names a romantic partner and an apartment. At least a dozen is a minimum number to consider in the authors illustration,not a request to purchase twelve homes or fabricate twelve relationships. The next paragraph raises practical burden,which remains context until separately targeted.

Final two evidence quotes stop after the second target sentence,leaving later unassigned demanding-heuristic discussion pending. All25 targets add exactly25 direct IDs; all previous published fingerprints remain unchanged.
